Best 8-Bay NAS for Media Libraries and Small Offices | ComputingForGeeks

 Eight bays is the point where the drives cost more than the NAS. Eight new 16TB WD Red Pro drives come to about $5,700. The boxes in this guide run from about $930 to $2,100 diskless, so the drives are 70 to 90 percent of every 16TB total we priced. Pick the 8-bay NAS for its CPU, network and warranty, then budget most of the money for disks.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 176358 
 We checked every price, seller and spec on October 21, 2026, against the maker spec sheets and the Amazon US listings. This is a spec-verified guide, not a hands-on test. The picks are split into two jobs: a big media library, where Quick Sync and capacity per dollar decide, and a small office, where ECC, ZFS or DSM and warranty length decide. For fewer drives, the 4-bay NAS guide covers the same ground one size down.
 8-bay NAS picks at a glance
 We ranked the six picks by job, with the diskless price band and the total once eight 16TB Red Pro drives are added. Usable space is the same 96 TB in RAID 6 on all of them, so the populated column is the real comparison:
 Pick Best for CPU Network ECC Box With 8x 16TB 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus Plex or Jellyfin library Core i5-1235U, Quick Sync 2x 10GbE No $1,350 to $1,400 about $7,100 
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G Cheap bulk storage ARM Alpine AL324 2x 10GbE SFP+, 2x 2.5GbE No $1,100 to $1,150 about $6,800 
 QNAP TS-873A-8G ZFS on a budget Ryzen V1500B 2x 2.5GbE, 10GbE by card Supported, ships non-ECC $1,400 to $1,450 about $7,150 
 Synology DS1825+ Windows and AD office Ryzen V1500B 2x 2.5GbE, 10GbE by card Yes $1,450 to $1,500 about $7,200 
 Synology DS1823xs+ Business-critical, 5-year warranty Ryzen V1780B 10GbE + 2x 1GbE Yes $2,000 to $2,100 about $7,750 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Rack in a UniFi network 4-core ARM Cortex-A57 2x 10G SFP+, 1x 10GbE No $930 to $960 about $6,650 
 Box prices differ by about $1,100 from the cheapest to the dearest. The spread between eight 12TB and eight 20TB drives is about $2,800, which is why the next section prices the drives before the box. All prices move during the 2026 shortage, so check the current price on Amazon before you order.
 How the numbers were collected
 Nothing here was benchmarked in our lab, so every figure has a source behind it. Each method below states where its numbers came from, and the sources file for this guide lists every page:
 Prices and sellers: the Amazon affiliate API on October 21, 2026, then a second check of the live product page with a US address, because the seller the API reports and the seller on the page disagreed for one pick.
 Specs: the maker spec page or datasheet first, then an independent review (ServeTheHome, NASCompares, ITPro, How-To Geek) where one exists.
 Usable capacity: RAID 6 keeps six of eight drives for data. The RAIDZ2 figure is 71.0 percent of raw, from the 8-wide row in our measured RAIDZ2 width table.
 Rebuild time: a floor computed as drive capacity divided by the maximum transfer rate in the WD datasheet, not a measured rebuild.
 Power figures are the makers’ own unless the text names a review, and not every maker says whether drives were fitted. The TS-832PX has no independent review at all, and the text says so where it matters.
 Step 1: Price the drives before the box
 New drives sold by Amazon itself came only from WD on the check date. Every new Seagate IronWolf Pro listing was a third-party seller with thin stock, and every Exos below $700 was renewed or recertified:
 Drive Per drive 8 drives RAID 6 usable Per usable TB 
 WD Red Pro 12TB $520 to $560 about $4,300 72 TB about $60 
 WD Red Pro 16TB $700 to $730 about $5,700 96 TB about $60 
 WD Red Pro 20TB $870 to $910 about $7,100 120 TB about $59 
 Seagate Exos X18 16TB, recertified $490 to $510 about $4,000 96 TB about $42 
 Cost per usable terabyte is nearly flat across the new Red Pro sizes: about $60 at 12TB and $59 at 20TB. Buy the capacity you need and not the size that looks cheaper per terabyte. The 12TB Red Pro is an air-filled drive rated at 34 dBA idle. The 16TB and 20TB helium models are rated at 20 dBA and draw 3.6 W idle against 6.1 W. In an office or under a desk, that makes 16TB the quieter floor.
 WD rates Red Plus for up to 8 bays and Red Pro for any bay count, so a full 8-bay box sits at the Red Plus ceiling. Red Plus is allowed, but Red Pro is the default we would buy for a box that runs office workloads around the clock. Our NAS hard drive guide ranks both by price per terabyte. Every drive here is CMR, which matters for the reasons in our CMR vs SMR explainer .
 Recertified drives cut the drive bill by about $1,700 on eight 16TB units. The trade is the warranty: the goHardDrive listing quotes a six-month Seagate replacement warranty, against five years on a new Red Pro. Our recertified drive guide covers when that trade makes sense, and a parity array with a second copy of the data is the case it fits.
 Step 2: Size the array for RAID 6 or RAIDZ2
 At eight drives of 12TB or more, RAID 6 or RAIDZ2 is the layout to run, because a rebuild reads every surviving drive end to end. The floor for that read, from the transfer rates WD rates them at, is half a day or more:
 Drive Rated max rate Rebuild floor RAID 6 usable RAIDZ2 reported 
 WD Red Pro 12TB 267 MB/s 12.5 h 72 TB (65.5 TiB) 68.2 TB 
 WD Red Pro 16TB 259 MB/s 17.2 h 96 TB (87.3 TiB) 90.9 TB 
 WD Red Pro 20TB 285 MB/s 19.5 h 120 TB (109.1 TiB) 113.6 TB 
 These floors assume the outer-track rate for the whole drive and no load from users, so real rebuilds run longer. A single-parity array spends that whole rebuild one drive failure from losing everything, which is the case against RAID 5 at these sizes.
 RAIDZ2 reports less space than RAID 6 for the same eight drives, 113.6 TB against 120 TB on 20TB disks, because of ZFS padding and the slop space ZFS reserves at the default record size. The full width table is in our RAIDZ2 drive count guide , where eight is also the widest vdev a single 8-port HBA can run.
 Eight 20TB drives also hit a Synology limit. Both Synology datasheets say a volume over 108 TB needs 32 GB of memory or more, and both boxes ship with 8 GB. A single 120 TB RAID 6 volume on either one means raising the RAM to its 32 GB maximum, or splitting the pool into two volumes.
 Step 3: Choose a box for a big media library
 A media library needs hardware transcoding for remote streams, enough network to move large files, and the lowest box price that still does both. Only one current desktop 8-bay box under $1,500 has an Intel iGPU with Quick Sync.
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus. About $1,350 to $1,400; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The DXP8800 Plus runs a 10-core Core i5-1235U with Iris Xe graphics, which gives it Quick Sync for Plex and Jellyfin. It ships with 8 GB of DDR5 (64 GB maximum), two 10GbE ports, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two NVMe slots, a PCIe x4 slot and a 128 GB boot SSD. UGREEN rates it at 70.39 W in access and 28.99 W with the drives hibernated, and sells it on Amazon itself.
 Drives: third-party drives are supported, with a compatibility list but no lock.
 Other operating systems: the UGREEN warranty page says the hardware warranty stays unchanged if you install a third-party system, which is why it is a common TrueNAS and Unraid box.
 Memory: the DDR5 is on-die ECC only. Intel lists no ECC support for the CPU, so this is not an ECC NAS.
 Warranty: 3 years under the UGREEN warranty policy, even though one block on the product page shows 2.
 Skip it if the data needs true ECC or a mature business suite. It is already the high-capacity pick in our Plex and Jellyfin NAS guide . The DXP Ultra guide covers the DXP8800 Ultra at about $1,750 to $1,800, which changes the CPU and the RAM ceiling (96 GB) and little else.
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G. About $1,100 to $1,150; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The TS-832PX is the cheapest desktop 8-bay box with 10GbE built in, with two 10GbE SFP+ ports and two 2.5GbE ports. Amazon sold it at about $1,100 to $1,150, with five left on the check date. QNAP rates it at 50.9 W typical and 27.9 W in standby with drives fitted.
 The CPU is a 4-core ARM Alpine AL324 at 1.7 GHz with 4 GB of non-ECC RAM in one slot (16 GB maximum), and it runs QTS only. That limits it to serving files: no transcoding, no ZFS, and little room for containers or VMs. Its single PCIe slot is Gen2 x2, and QNAP itself notes that a card there will restrict 10GbE performance. The warranty is 2 years, against 3 on the UGREEN, DS1825+ and TS-873A and 5 on the DS1823xs+. We also found no independent review of it. We kept it as a pick anyway. QNAP publishes full specs and power figures, and it is the only desktop 8-bay with 10GbE at this price.
 Anything on the box that needs a CPU rules it out. Buy it as a backup target or a bulk media share whose players do their own decoding.
 Step 4: Choose a box for a small office
 An office box is judged on what happens when something fails: ECC memory, a file system with snapshots, a warranty that covers the service life, and a supported upgrade path to 10GbE. Four picks cover that, from a budget ZFS box to a rack unit for UniFi sites.
 QNAP TS-873A-8G
 QNAP TS-873A-8G. About $1,400 to $1,450; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The TS-873A is the cheapest pick here with ZFS and an ECC-capable CPU. It runs a 4-core Ryzen Embedded V1500B with 8 GB of RAM (64 GB maximum). It boots QTS or QuTS hero, the QNAP ZFS system with snapshots and inline compression. Two PCIe Gen3 x4 slots take a 10GbE card and a second card; the onboard ports are two 2.5GbE.
 ServeTheHome measured 26 W idle with no drives and a 58 W maximum in its 2021 review, and QNAP rates it at 54.1 W typical with drives. The platform dates from 2021, and its two M.2 slots are Gen3 x1, so NVMe cache is slow. The stock 8 GB is not ECC. QNAP says ECC memory requires removing the pre-installed modules, because ECC and non-ECC cannot be mixed, so matched ECC SODIMMs are an extra cost on top of the box price. Price a 10GbE card from the QNAP compatibility list in from the start too, and plan for 16 GB of RAM for ZFS deduplication; ITPro recommends 32 GB for QuTS hero once 10GbE is added.
 Look elsewhere if you want ECC or 10GbE without extra parts, or fast M.2 storage.
 Synology DS1825+
 Synology DS1825+. About $1,450 to $1,500; check the current price and seller on Amazon. 
 The DS1825+ is the pick for an office that already runs Active Directory and wants DSM. It has the same Ryzen V1500B as the TS-873A, with 8 GB of ECC DDR4 (32 GB maximum) and two 2.5GbE ports. Two NVMe slots and a PCIe Gen3 slot with an x4 link for a 10GbE or 25GbE card complete it. Two DX525 expansion units take it to 18 bays, and Synology rates it at 60.1 W in access.
 On DSM 7.3 or later, the 2025 Plus models accept unlisted hard drives for new pools again. Unlisted M.2 drives are still limited to migration, with no new pool or cache, so buy Synology SSDs if you want NVMe cache. The full policy is on the Synology drive compatibility page , and our Synology alternative guide compares it with the other vendors.
 On the check date, the page seller was RockyStone Electronics, a third party, at about $1,450 to $1,500. The Amazon catalogue listed Amazon as the merchant at the same time. Check who sells it before you order, and buy from an authorized Synology reseller if warranty support matters. Our small business NAS guide covers the DSM and AD setup, and the neo+ vs Plus comparison covers the cheaper DS1825neo+.
 Synology DS1823xs+
 Synology DS1823xs+. About $2,000 to $2,100; check the current price on Amazon. 
 About $600 more than the DS1825+ buys three things: a 5-year warranty, a faster 4-core Ryzen V1780B, and 10GbE on the board next to two 1GbE ports and a management port. It has 8 GB of ECC memory (32 GB maximum), the same Gen3 slot with an x4 link, and 18 bays with two DX517 units. Synology rates it at 87.93 W in access. Amazon sells it directly.
 As a 2023 xs model, it is outside the 2025 drive policy change, because Synology says that change does not apply retroactively. Owners report “unverified” warnings in DSM when they fit third-party drives. It also has no SHR, only standard RAID levels.
 Pass on it if you plan to fill it with WD or Seagate drives and do not want those warnings, or if anything needs transcoding.
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8. About $930 to $960 from a third-party seller on Amazon; check the current price. 
 UniFi built the cheapest box here and the only rack unit among the picks: 2U, 480 mm deep, with rails in the box. It has two 10G SFP+ ports and one 10GbE RJ45 port, a 4-core ARM Cortex-A57 with 16 GB of soldered RAM, and two hot-swap power supply bays. NASCompares measured about 800 to 850 MB/s sequential read from eight 8TB drives in RAID 5.
 Price: Ubiquiti lists it at about $800 before a checkout surcharge. On Amazon it comes from a third-party seller at about $930 to $960 on October 21, 2026; check the current price.
 Power: one 550 W supply is included, and the second for redundancy costs about $159.
 Storage: RAID 5, 6 or 10 with a hot spare, shared over SMB and NFS. There is no iSCSI and no app or container platform, and the trays for its two M.2 cache slots are sold separately.
 Warranty: the UI Store page lists no base term, only UI Care, which extends cover to 5 years for about $199. US resellers list a 1-year limited warranty, which would make it the shortest base cover here.
 Skip it if you need Docker, iSCSI, ECC or any software outside UniFi Drive. Buy it if the rack already holds UniFi gear; our first rackmount server guide covers depth and rails for a home rack.
 Step 5: Price a DIY 8-bay build
 A DIY build with Quick Sync and eight SATA ports on the board costs about the same as the DXP8800 Plus at current DDR5 prices. This basket uses a Jonsbo N3 case and a Mini-ITX board with eight SATA ports, so no HBA is needed:
 Part Pick Band 
 Case Jonsbo N3, 8 hot-swap bays about $160 
 Board StoneStorm Q670 Mini-ITX, 8 SATA about $210 
 CPU Intel Core i5-14400 about $210 
 Memory Crucial Pro 2×16 GB DDR5-6000 about $540 
 Power Cooler Master V750 SFX Gold about $125 
 Boot WD Green SN3000 500 GB about $95 
 10GbE TP-Link TX401 about $60 
 We priced the basket at about $1,400 for 32 GB of RAM, against 8 GB in the DXP8800 Plus at about the same price. A lean version with 16 GB and a Core i3-14100 comes to about $1,050 to $1,100, though the i3 was listed for a later ship date. Several parts were sold by third parties with thin stock. The specs for the board come from its Amazon listing only, and that listing does not state the PCIe slot, so confirm it before you buy the 10GbE card.
 DIY no longer saves money at this size, so build one for the freedom to run any OS. Unraid at eight drives also needs its Unleashed licence, about $109, on top of the basket. There is also no ECC on a Q670 board. The case options are in our NAS case guide , the power and cost comparison is in DIY NAS vs prebuilt , and the OS choice is in TrueNAS vs Unraid .
 Step 6: Match the network to the array
 Eight hard drives in a parity array read faster than a 2.5GbE port can carry. NASCompares measured 800 to 850 MB/s from eight 8TB drives in RAID 5 on the UNAS Pro 8. A 2.5GbE link tops out near 280 MB/s, so a 2.5GbE-only box leaves most of the array idle on large transfers.
 10GbE on the board: DXP8800 Plus, TS-832PX, DS1823xs+ and UNAS Pro 8. On the DXP8800 Ultra, ITPro measured 9.2 Gbit/s read and 8.8 Gbit/s write in the Iometer synthetic test, and 3.8 and 3.0 Gbit/s copying a 25 GB file.
 10GbE by card: TS-873A and DS1825+. Use a card from the QNAP or Synology compatibility list for each box.
 The switch: a 10GbE NAS needs a 10GbE port at the other end, which our 10GbE switch guide covers.
 A 1GbE or 2.5GbE network is fine for streaming, because a single 4K stream needs a small fraction of either. The 10GbE port pays off on backups, video editing and VM storage, and the box belongs on a UPS whichever network it runs, as our NAS UPS guide explains.
 Models we left out and why
 Several 8-bay boxes looked right in a search and failed a check. Each one is excluded for a specific, verifiable reason:
 QNAP TS-855X: the Amazon title says 8 bays, but the box has six 3.5-inch bays and two 2.5-inch bays.
 Synology DS1821+: discontinued. Its US product page now redirects to the download center, and the remaining Amazon listings are third-party bundles above $3,700.
 Asustor Lockerstor 8 Gen3 (AS6808T): true ECC and 10GbE, but about $1,820 or more everywhere, third-party only on Amazon, and no written independent review.
 TerraMaster U8-500 Plus: a 2U unit with a Core i7-1255U and 10GbE at about $1,530, but no independent review we could find, and its RAID grows only by swapping in larger drives, not by adding drives.
 TerraMaster U8-423: a 2U unit with a Celeron N5095 that does hardware transcoding, two 2.5GbE ports and a 2-year warranty, at about $825 direct from TerraMaster but not sold on Amazon US.
 TerraMaster F8 SSD: all-flash, covered in our all-flash NAS guide .
 QNAP TVS-h874 and TS-855eU: out of stock or used only on the check date.
 QNAP also previewed an 8-bay AI NAS at Computex in June 2026 without US availability, so it is not in this guide until it ships. Past eight drives, the next step is an expansion unit or a DAS or JBOD enclosure , not a bigger NAS.

results.title: Best 8-Bay NAS for Small Business 2026: 3 Systems Compared | iFeeltech

Best 8-Bay NAS for Small Business 2026: 3 Systems Compared | iFeeltech 
 Skip to main content 
 Eight drive bays do more than fill out a spec sheet. They let a business maintain two-drive fault tolerance without surrendering most of its capacity to parity, delay the next storage migration by years, and sustain larger backup or media workflows without running out of headroom. They also raise the stakes of a platform decision. Eight NAS drives, a network upgrade and an independent backup target often add up to more than the enclosure itself.
 We compare three systems using the same drive set and the same protection assumptions: UGREEN's DXP8800 Plus for hardware density and performance, Synology's DS1825+ for software depth and recovery tooling, and UniFi's UNAS Pro 8 for simple high-capacity storage inside an existing UniFi environment. The right answer is not the box with the fastest CPU — it is the one that can store, protect and restore the workload your team actually runs.
 Affiliate Disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. If you make a purchase through these links, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate, iFeelTech earns from qualifying purchases.
 Methodology and Scope
 This is an editorial comparison based on verified vendor documentation, current US retail pricing and our deployment experience — we did not benchmark all three systems side by side in a lab for this article. Specifications, software capabilities and prices were verified against manufacturer product pages and authorized retailers on September 21, 2026. Firmware versions were not controlled.
 Why these three and not QNAP, Asustor or TerraMaster? These are the three 8-bay platforms we see most often in small-business projects across our client base: UGREEN for hardware value, Synology for business software maturity and UniFi for teams already standardized on Ubiquiti infrastructure. QNAP, Asustor and TerraMaster make competitive 8-bay products; they are not covered here because each would require its own platform evaluation. If your shortlist includes them, our best NAS for small business roundup provides broader category coverage.
 Fast Verdict: Which 8-Bay NAS — and Do You Need One?
 Three Systems, One Drive Set
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus ($1,370) — Best included hardware for technical teams that need dual 10GbE, Thunderbolt 4 and compute headroom without add-on cards. Least mature backup and administration suite of the three.
 Synology DS1825+ (~$1,250) — Best software for business data protection, automated backup across endpoints, and low-touch administration. Requires a ~$258 add-in card for 10GbE. Expandable to 18 drives.
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 ($799) — Lowest enclosure cost with included 10GbE and redundant power, managed from the same console as your switches and access points. No Docker, no VMs, no app ecosystem — file storage and backup only.
 Stay with 4 or 5 bays if your total data fits comfortably in a single-parity array today, you have no plan for independent backup, no need for 10GbE and no one to administer the system. A larger enclosure does not solve a missing backup strategy.
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus Synology DS1825+ UniFi UNAS Pro 8 
 Street price (diskless) $1,370 ~$1,250 $799

 10GbE 2× included Optional PCIe card 2× SFP+ + 1× RJ45

 Form factor Desktop Desktop 2U rackmount 
 Expansion None Up to 18 drives (2× DX525) None 
 Capacity Before Brand: What Eight Bays Actually Give You
 Before comparing platforms, understand what eight bays can and cannot do.
 Raw capacity is the sum of drive sizes — eight 20TB drives provide 160TB of raw decimal storage. That number appears on the box but is not the usable figure — you need to subtract what protection costs.
 One-disk parity (RAID 5) dedicates one drive's worth of capacity to parity data, leaving seven drives usable. You survive a single drive failure. With 20TB drives, that is roughly 127 TiB (~140TB) of usable space.
 Two-disk parity (RAID 6 or SHR-2) dedicates two drives to parity, leaving six usable. You survive two simultaneous drive failures. With 20TB drives: roughly 109 TiB (~120TB) usable. This is the practical advantage of eight bays — you can afford two-disk fault tolerance and still have meaningful storage. Our RAID level comparison covers how each level handles drive failures and rebuilds.
 A hot spare reserves one additional drive that automatically replaces a failed member. In an eight-drive RAID 6 with a hot spare, five drives hold data, two hold parity and one waits. That costs another 20TB of capacity but starts rebuilding immediately.
 RAID Is Not Backup
 Two-disk parity protects against drive failure. It does not protect against accidental deletion, ransomware encryption, theft, fire, firmware corruption or administrator error. Every 8-bay NAS in this comparison needs an independent backup target — a second NAS, an external drive, or a cloud destination — before it is protecting business data. Our 3-2-1 backup rule guide covers how to plan this properly. Budget for it.
 TB vs TiB: Drive manufacturers use decimal terabytes (1TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes). Operating systems report binary tebibytes (1 TiB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes). A "20TB" drive shows as approximately 18.19 TiB in your NAS dashboard. This is not missing space — it is a unit difference. The worksheet below uses both.
 Filesystem overhead: Every NAS filesystem reserves space for metadata, internal structures, snapshot tracking and other system functions. The exact amount depends on filesystem type (Btrfs, ext4), RAID implementation, firmware version, enabled features (snapshots, quotas, deduplication) and vendor-specific allocations. Expect the displayed usable capacity after volume creation to be noticeably lower than the raw RAID math — verify it on your chosen platform and firmware before committing to a capacity plan.
 Same Drives, Same Protection, Honest Math
 This worksheet uses eight Seagate IronWolf Pro 20TB (ST20000NT001) drives — the current-generation CMR NAS drive rated for 550TB/year workload with a five-year warranty and three years of Rescue Data Recovery Services. We use $600 per drive as a planning assumption in the cost tables below. Current new-retail offers vary substantially by retailer, seller, condition and warranty eligibility — established sellers were listing $670–$730 at the time of writing, while marketplace sellers started lower. At $670 per drive, the eight-drive set costs $5,360 instead of $4,800 — a $560 difference that shifts every system total upward equally. Verify the exact SKU, seller and warranty before purchasing. Do not confuse this model with the older ST20000NE000 (300TB/year workload rating), which is still sold alongside it.
 Drive compatibility varies by platform:
 Synology: DSM 7.3 permits non-validated third-party HDDs in 2025 DS Plus models for new storage pools and migration. Drives not on Synology's compatibility list may appear as unverified, and drive-related technical support may be limited. Synology's own HAT-series drives receive the deepest validation and full support guarantee. Verify the complete drive model number on the DS1825+ compatibility list before purchasing.
 UGREEN: Supports third-party drives from Seagate, WD and Toshiba, but advises buyers to verify the complete part number on its compatibility list before purchasing.
 UniFi: Requires 1TB-or-larger, 7200 RPM CMR drives for multi-bay RAID — a broader requirement than model-specific validation.

 With identical drives and equivalent two-disk parity, all three systems provide approximately 109 TiB before filesystem and metadata overhead — about 120TB in marketing terms. The displayed capacity after volume creation will be somewhat lower; verify it on the chosen platform and firmware. The difference between these products is not capacity. It is what happens to the data after it lands on the drives.
 RAID 5 Alternative
 If you accept single-disk fault tolerance, RAID 5 yields roughly 127 TiB (~140TB) before overhead — about 20% more usable space. That comes with higher rebuild risk: if a second drive fails during the rebuild of a first failure, you lose the array. With 20TB drives, rebuilds are a prolonged process — the exact duration depends on drive condition, array load, RAID implementation, background tasks and rebuild priority settings. For business data, we recommend RAID 6 or SHR-2 in an 8-bay configuration.
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus: Maximum Included Hardware for Technical Teams
 The DXP8800 Plus has the strongest CPU and the most included connectivity of these three systems. The Intel Core i5-1235U is a 10-core/12-thread laptop-class processor better suited to mixed compute and storage workloads than either the Synology's embedded AMD or the UniFi's ARM chip. Dual 10GbE ports are built in — no adapter card, no extra cost — and support link aggregation for higher aggregate multi-client throughput when your switch supports it. (Link aggregation improves total bandwidth across multiple connections and provides failover; a single file transfer from one client does not automatically double in speed.) Two Thunderbolt 4 ports (40Gbps interface each) allow direct-connect workflows for video teams, though actual throughput depends on the RAID array speed, SMB stack and client configuration — not only the interface rating.
 Where this hardware matters: A video production team editing 4K or 6K footage directly from the NAS over Thunderbolt 4 or 10GbE. A small architecture or design firm running large Revit models from shared storage. A technical team using Docker containers and VMs alongside file storage. The DXP8800 Plus has the compute, memory headroom (expandable to 64GB DDR5) and I/O ports to support these workloads — though concurrent performance under mixed loads depends on memory, disk IOPS and application demands, not only the CPU.
 Where UGOS Pro falls short: UGREEN's operating system handles file sharing, Docker, virtual machines and AI-powered photo management. What it does not match is Synology's application depth for business operations. Synology's Active Backup suite — Active Backup for Business for computers, physical servers and VMware/Hyper-V VMs, plus the separate Active Backup for Microsoft 365 package for Exchange Online, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams — has no UGOS equivalent. Hyper Backup's versioned, encrypted, deduplicated backup to dozens of cloud and local targets is more mature than what UGOS Pro currently offers. Snapshot Replication with immutable snapshots is more mature in DSM. If your business requires turnkey endpoint backup or compliance-oriented data protection, UGOS Pro requires more testing, more workarounds, or different third-party tools.
 UGREEN also sells the newer DXP8800 Ultra ($1,780) , which upgrades the processor to an Intel Core 7 150U and supports up to 96GB DDR5 RAM. For most file-serving and backup workloads, the Plus at $1,370 delivers the same capacity and connectivity. The Ultra makes sense for teams running compute-heavy containers, local AI workloads, or multiple simultaneous 10GbE video streams where the workload is demonstrably CPU-bound. Do not upgrade to the Ultra solely for file storage — the Plus already exceeds what the drives can deliver.
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus Verdict
 Best fit: Creative teams, technical users and businesses with validated workflows that need 10GbE, Thunderbolt 4 and compute headroom included in the box price.
 Disqualifier: The business expects turnkey backup, compliance tools or a polished administration experience without testing and validation. UGOS Pro is capable but not as mature as DSM for business administration.
 Synology DS1825+: The Recovery and Administration Choice
 The DS1825+ takes a different approach — less hardware per dollar, substantially more software per dollar. The AMD Ryzen V1500B is a 2018-era quad-core embedded processor that does not match the UGREEN's i5-1235U in raw compute. But DSM is the most mature NAS operating system on the market, and for business data protection, that maturity is often worth the trade-off.
 Active Backup for Business provides centralized, license-free backup for Windows PCs, Linux servers, and VMware/Hyper-V virtual machines. The separate Active Backup for Microsoft 365 package handles Exchange Online, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams — also license-free. Together, they consolidate endpoint, VM and SaaS backups on one Synology appliance, with separate management interfaces for the two packages and granular file-level or bare-metal restore. For a business protecting 25–75 endpoints plus Microsoft 365 accounts, this software suite alone can justify the Synology premium over competing hardware.
 Hyper Backup handles NAS-to-NAS and NAS-to-cloud backup with versioning, client-side encryption, deduplication and integrity checks. It supports Synology C2, Backblaze B2, Amazon S3, Azure, Google Cloud and more. Snapshot Replication provides immutable, scheduled snapshots with offsite replication — a defense against ransomware that does not depend on a separate backup application.
 The networking cost: The DS1825+ includes dual 2.5GbE ports. For a small team doing office file access, that is adequate. For video editing, large database workloads, or multi-user concurrent access to large files, you need the Synology E10G30-T2 dual-port 10GbE adapter at approximately $258 (Newegg, September 2026). That card uses the DS1825+'s PCIe Gen3 x8 slot (running at x4 link speed). It works, it is reliable, and it is an additional cost that the UGREEN and UniFi units do not require. For a deeper comparison of UGREEN and Synology across multiple bay counts, see our UGREEN vs Synology NAS platform comparison .
 Expansion: The DS1825+ supports two DX525 expansion units, scaling to 18 total drives (360TB raw with 20TB drives). No other unit in this comparison offers expansion beyond eight bays. If you expect to outgrow eight bays within three years, Synology is the only platform here that can grow without replacing the enclosure.
 Synology DS1825+ Verdict
 Best fit: Businesses that need protected, administrated data — automated endpoint backup, immutable snapshots, granular permissions and monitoring — with low ongoing administration overhead.
 Disqualifier: 10GbE is essential and the add-in card cost breaks the budget, or the business prioritizes raw compute and direct-connect I/O over software depth.
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8: Simple Rack Storage for a UniFi Environment
 The UNAS Pro 8 costs $799 — nearly half the UGREEN and roughly $450 less than the Synology before any networking add-ons. It is a 2U rackmount appliance with dual redundant hot-swap power supplies, an ARM Cortex-A57 processor, 16GB of fixed RAM, and three 10G ports (two SFP+, one RJ45). It appears in your UniFi console alongside your switches, access points and cameras.
 That console integration is the primary value proposition. An IT administrator managing a UniFi network does not need to learn a second platform, bookmark a second management URL or maintain separate credentials for storage. The UNAS Pro 8 shows up in Site Manager with drive health, RAID status and storage utilization visible from the same dashboard that monitors your network.
 What UniFi Drive does: SMB file sharing, user and group permissions, RAID 5/6/10, scheduled snapshots, storage-pool encryption, Time Machine backup targets, backup to a remote UNAS, backup to CIFS/SMB servers, and backup to cloud services including Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Amazon S3, Backblaze B2 and Wasabi. That covers straightforward file storage and backup workflows.
 What UniFi Drive does not do (as of September 2026): No Docker containers. No virtual machines. No iSCSI. No application hosting. No package manager or app store. No centralized endpoint backup comparable to Synology's Active Backup suite. No sophisticated versioned backup with deduplication. UniFi Drive is actively evolving — verify current capabilities before purchasing. For a detailed analysis of what UniFi Drive can and cannot replace, see our UniFi NAS vs Synology feature comparison and UniFi NAS complete business guide .
 The rack requirement: This is a 2U rackmount unit. It is designed for an equipment rack rather than a quiet office. If you do not have a rack or dedicated equipment closet, the UNAS Pro 8 is not the right form factor. For a quieter 4-bay desktop option in the UniFi ecosystem, see the UNAS 4 .
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Verdict
 Best fit: A team already running UniFi infrastructure that needs straightforward high-capacity file storage and backup, managed from one console, with included 10GbE and redundant power at the lowest enclosure cost.
 Disqualifier: The business needs Docker, VMs, centralized endpoint backup, application hosting, or any workflow that UniFi Drive does not support as of September 2026.
 Complete-System Cost: Enclosure Is the Cheapest Part
 The enclosure is typically the smallest line item. The table below uses identical drives and two-disk parity for all three systems. Prices are US street prices checked September 21, 2026.

The $600-per-drive figure is a planning assumption rather than a quoted authorized-retailer price. Established sellers were listing the Seagate IronWolf Pro 20TB (ST20000NT001) around $670–$730 in September 2026, while some marketplace offers were lower. Verify the exact SKU, condition, seller and warranty eligibility before purchasing. The E10G30-T2 adapter price is from Newegg ($258).
 Workload Verdicts
 Every recommendation below states the dependency that could reverse it.
 1. General Office Files and PC/Server Backup
 Synology DS1825+. Active Backup for Business provides centralized, license-free backup for Windows PCs and file servers from one console. DSM handles SMB permissions, quota management, Active Directory integration and scheduled snapshots. Reversal: if no endpoints require centralized backup and the team already manages UniFi infrastructure, the UNAS Pro 8 handles basic file storage at lower cost. 
 2. Microsoft 365 Protection
 Synology DS1825+. Active Backup for Microsoft 365 backs up Exchange Online, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams data to local storage — no per-seat licensing fee. Reversal: if the Microsoft 365 backup requirement is limited to OneDrive for Business, UniFi Drive now supports OneDrive backup natively. For Exchange, SharePoint and Teams, Synology remains the only self-hosted option in this comparison. 
 3. Video Editing Over 10GbE
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus. Dual 10GbE and dual Thunderbolt 4 are included — no adapter cards required. The Intel i5-1235U is better suited to concurrent thumbnail generation and background indexing than the other CPUs in this comparison. Reversal: if the editing workflow relies on software only available on DSM (specific Synology packages or tested integrations), add a 10GbE card to the DS1825+ instead. 
 4. Surveillance Archive / Backup Target
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 if you are already running UniFi Protect — the UNAS can serve as an archive target within the same console. Synology DS1825+ if you need Surveillance Station's support for up to 40 cameras and integration with 8,700+ third-party IP camera models. Note: the DS1825+ includes only two camera licenses; additional cameras require purchased licenses. Advanced AI analytics (people counting, intrusion detection) may require compatible cameras or Synology's dedicated DVA hardware rather than the DS1825+ alone. Reversal: see our UniFi Protect vs Synology Surveillance Station comparison for a detailed breakdown. 
 5. Virtual Machines and Containers
 Synology DS1825+ for tested, documented VM and Docker workflows through Virtual Machine Manager and Container Manager. UGREEN DXP8800 Plus for raw compute advantage — the i5-1235U and 64GB RAM ceiling handle heavier container workloads. The UNAS Pro 8 does not support VMs or containers. Reversal: if the container workload demands more CPU than the Synology's V1500B can deliver, UGREEN offers stronger hardware despite less mature orchestration tooling. 
 6. Existing UniFi Rack
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8. It occupies 2U in the rack you already own, connects to the SFP+ ports on your existing UniFi switches, and is managed from the console your team already uses. Reversal: if the workload requires applications, endpoint backup or VM hosting that UniFi Drive does not support, the UNAS Pro 8 as a file tier plus a separate Synology or UGREEN unit for applications may be the right combination. 
 7. Business With No Dedicated IT
 Synology DS1825+. DSM's guided setup, automated backup scheduling, health monitoring with email alerts, and extensive documentation make it the most approachable platform for a business without full-time IT staff. Synology's support ecosystem (knowledge base, community forums, professional services through partners) is deeper than UGREEN's or Ubiquiti's for NAS-specific issues. Reversal: if the business already has a managed IT provider fluent in UniFi, the UNAS Pro 8's console integration may reduce support overhead. 
 Migration and Exit Costs
 Switching NAS platforms is not a firmware update. Budget for these:
 Data migration time. Copying 100TB over a single 10GbE link at a sustained rate of 400–600 MB/s takes roughly 48–72 hours of raw transfer time — before accounting for interruptions, verification passes and small-file overhead that will extend it further. During migration, you need both the old and new systems running simultaneously with enough capacity to hold the complete dataset. Plan for temporary double storage.
 Permissions and shares. SMB share structures, user accounts, group memberships and ACLs do not transfer automatically between Synology DSM, UGOS Pro and UniFi Drive. Rebuild them manually or script the migration. Active Directory integration helps if both old and new systems join the same domain.
 Application state. Docker containers, VMs, backup job configurations, scheduled tasks and surveillance recordings are platform-specific. Plan to recreate rather than migrate these. Export configurations where possible and test the new setup before decommissioning the old.
 Drive portability. Do not assume you can move a RAID array from one vendor's enclosure to another. RAID metadata formats differ between platforms. The safe migration path is always: copy all data to the new system, verify the copy, validate access and permissions, then decommission the old system. Moving a live disk set between vendors risks data loss unless the vendor explicitly documents support for that exact migration.
 User retraining. If your team accesses files through vendor-specific client apps (Synology Drive, UGREEN's mobile app, UniFi's drive client), switching platforms means new software on every workstation and phone. Factor in the support tickets.
 Final Buying Decision
 Come back to three questions:
 1. Which restore job matters most? If restoring a failed PC, a corrupted VM or a deleted SharePoint site needs to work on the first attempt, Synology's Active Backup ecosystem is the answer. If the restore requirement is "get the shared files back," any of these three handle that.
 2. Who administers it? If a non-technical office manager monitors storage, Synology's DSM is the most approachable. If a UniFi-certified IT provider manages the network, the UNAS Pro 8 reduces their tool count. If an in-house technical team validates their own workflows, UGREEN's hardware advantage lets them build exactly what they need.
 3. What network throughput do you genuinely need? A five-person accounting firm accessing office documents, PDFs and archived records does not need 10GbE. A video team pulling 4K ProRes from shared storage is likely to benefit from it. Match the investment to the real workflow — not the theoretical maximum.
 Buy the system that answers all three honestly.
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus — $1,370 Synology DS1825+ — ~$1,250 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 — $799

 Frequently Asked Questions
 How much usable storage does an 8-bay NAS actually provide? 
 With eight 20TB drives in a two-disk fault-tolerant configuration (RAID 6 or SHR-2), you get roughly 109 TiB of raw usable capacity before filesystem overhead — about 120TB in marketing terms. That is six drives worth of data, with two drives worth of parity protection. The actual displayed capacity will be somewhat lower after filesystem metadata, snapshot reserves and vendor-specific overhead — verify the final figure on your chosen platform after volume creation.
 Is an 8-bay NAS overkill for a small business? 
 It depends on your data growth and protection requirements. If you need two-disk fault tolerance (protection against two simultaneous drive failures) plus room for years of growth, eight bays make practical sense. If your total data is under 20TB and a single-parity RAID in a 4-bay unit covers it, start there. Eight bays cost more in drives, network upgrades and power than most people budget for.
 Do I need 10GbE with an 8-bay NAS? 
 For single-user office file access, 2.5GbE is sufficient. If multiple users access the NAS simultaneously or anyone works with large video, design or database files, 10GbE prevents the network from becoming the bottleneck before the drives do. All three 8-bay NAS units compared here support 10GbE — UGREEN and UniFi include it, while Synology requires a separate adapter card.
 Can I use non-Synology drives in the DS1825+? 
 Yes. With the DSM 7.3 update, Synology permits non-validated third-party HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs in 2025 Plus-series models including the DS1825+ for storage pool creation. Drives not on Synology's compatibility list may appear as unverified and drive-related support may be limited, but the previous drive-lockdown policy has been reversed. Synology's own HAT-series drives receive the deepest validation and full support guarantee.
 Does the UniFi UNAS Pro 8 run Docker or virtual machines? 
 No. UniFi Drive is a file storage and backup platform supporting SMB shares, snapshots, encryption, Time Machine, and cloud backup to services like Backblaze B2 and Google Drive. It does not support Docker containers, virtual machines, iSCSI or application hosting. If those are requirements, consider the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus or Synology DS1825+.
 Which 8-bay NAS is best for video editing? 
 The UGREEN DXP8800 Plus, primarily because its dual 10GbE ports and dual Thunderbolt 4 ports are included — no adapter cards or SFP+ transceivers required. The Intel i5-1235U processor also handles thumbnail generation and metadata indexing more capably than the ARM or older AMD processors in the other two units.

Best 8-Bay NAS (2026): The One I Run and the One I'd Buy - WunderTech 
 Skip to content 
 Post author: Frank Joseph 
 Post published: April 17, 2023 
 Post last modified: September 28, 2026 
 Post category: Home Lab Hardware 
 Reading time: 11 mins read
 If you’re buying new today, the best 8 bay NAS for most people is the UGREEN DXP8800 Ultra , and it’s the one I’d buy. If you already own the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus , I would not upgrade. I use one as my offsite backup, it’s been rock solid for close to a year, and the Ultra is really just a refresh of it.
 The other two picks depend on what you want the NAS to do. The UniFi UNAS Pro 8 is the rackmount, storage-only option, and it’s one I’ve benchmarked myself and use for backup storage. The Synology DS1825+ is the 8-bay NAS for anyone who wants Synology DSM, though its drive policy is worth reading first. And if you’re only starting with four drives, a six-bay is usually the better buy.
 Disclosure: Some links below are affiliate links, which means that I earn a percentage of each sale at no cost to you. UGREEN sent me the DXP8800 Ultra and has sponsored several of my videos. Thank you for your support. 
 Here’s how my four picks and two other 8-bay options compare on the specs that differ.
 NAS CPU RAM (standard / max) Networking M.2 slots Worth knowing 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Ultra Intel Core 7 150U 8 GB DDR5 / 96 GB 2x 10GbE, 2x Thunderbolt 4 2 PCIe Gen4 x4 slot 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus Intel Core i5-1235U 8 GB DDR5 / 64 GB 2x 10GbE, 2x Thunderbolt 4 2 PCIe x4 slot 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 16 GB 2x 10G SFP+, 1x 10GbE 2 2U rackmount, storage only 
 Synology DS1825+ AMD Ryzen V1500B 8 GB DDR4 ECC / 32 GB 2x 2.5GbE 2 (Synology SSDs) Expands to 18 bays 
 QNAP TS-873A AMD Ryzen V1500B 8 GB / 64 GB 2x 2.5GbE 2 QTS or ZFS-based QuTS hero 
 Asustor AS6808T AMD Ryzen Embedded V3C14 16 GB DDR5 ECC / 64 GB 2x 10GbE, 2x 5GbE 4 2x USB4 
 Table of Contents

 Do You Need 8 Bays, or Is a 6-Bay Enough? 
 The Best 8-Bay NAS I’d Buy Today 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Ultra: Best 8-Bay NAS for a New Buyer 
 Intel Core 7 150U · 8 GB DDR5 (96 GB max) · 2x 10GbE · 2x Thunderbolt 4 · 8 bays + 2 M.2
 If you’re a new buyer, this is the device that I’d buy. It’s the most expensive of my four picks, and UGREEN sells it as a small-business NAS, but it’s a great fit at home for anyone who wants the top end.
 Check price at Amazon → 
 UGREEN sent me this one for review, but the recommendation comes from my own testing.
 Compared to the DXP8800 Plus, the CPU went from the i5-1235U to the Core 7 150U, and the memory ceiling went from 64 GB to 96 GB. The ports are basically the same, with two 10GbE ports, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, eight SATA bays, two M.2 slots and a PCIe x4 slot.
 I had no problem loading it with eight drives, no SSD cache, and editing directly off of it, which is saying something because not all devices are capable of that. I also ran the same large-file copy over 10GbE on the Ultra and on a 12-bay DIY build I’ve been testing, and they were practically even. If you don’t have a 10GbE network yet, the two Thunderbolt 4 ports give a single computer a direct-attach option instead.
 It ships with UGOS Pro, which runs Docker and virtual machines, and UGREEN allows third-party drives and operating systems like TrueNAS or Unraid. UGOS backs up to another UGREEN NAS or an rsync server, and its Cloud Drives app adds Amazon S3 and Backblaze backup.
 The One I Run: UGREEN DXP8800 Plus 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus: Best for an Offsite Backup NAS 
 Intel Core i5-1235U · 8 GB DDR5 (64 GB max) · 2x 10GbE · 2x Thunderbolt 4 · 8 bays + 2 M.2
 I’m using a DXP8800 Plus as an offsite backup, and it’s been absolutely rock solid for close to a year, maybe even over a year at this point. It’s still sold new and sits below the Ultra in price, so it’s a great 8-bay NAS if you don’t need the newer CPU.
 Check price at UGREEN → 
 Back in November 2025, I called it the best off-site NAS backup that I have ever had, and nothing since has changed my mind. When I first set it up, it ran UGOS, and I used UGREEN’s default rsync backup tool to pull data from my onsite NAS devices with snapshots on top.
 The problem was that I wanted all of that data encrypted at rest, and it wasn’t. So I installed TrueNAS Community Edition on the DXP8800 Plus to use ZFS replication instead. As of January 2026, it pulled a ZFS replication every hour, so no credentials for the backup box sat on the onsite NAS, and Proxmox Backup Server ran on it as a VM, which worked well. Security changes over time and nothing is guaranteed, but encryption was why I switched.
 That’s the part of UGREEN I’d point out to anyone who likes to tinker, since the hardware doesn’t lock you into UGOS. It’s also one of the reasons UGREEN is on my list of the best Synology NAS alternatives . If you put TrueNAS on a DXP8800 Plus with eight drives, you’re probably going to be using RAID-Z2.
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8: The Rackmount Pick 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8: Best Rackmount, Storage-Only NAS 
 2U rackmount · quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 · 16 GB RAM · 2x 10G SFP+ and 1x 10GbE · 8 bays + 2 M.2 · 2 power supply slots, 1 included
 The UNAS Pro 8 is the cheapest of my four picks, and I use one as backup storage, with every app I run on separate hardware. As of August 2026, it’s storage only, with no Docker, no virtual machines and no apps. It ships with one power module for its two slots .
 Check price at the UniFi Store → 
 The UNAS Pro 8 is the only rackmount 8-bay NAS here, and UniFi lists its rails for square-hole, four-post racks with posts 600 to 1066 mm apart. I tested it against the seven-bay UNAS Pro in September 2025 on an early-access version of UniFi Drive, so the numbers may have moved since. I started with four 8 TB drives in RAID 5 plus two M.2 SSDs as SSD cache, against the UNAS Pro running six drives in RAID 10. The UNAS Pro 8 won on small files, while the UNAS Pro stayed slightly ahead on sustained large-file reads.
 When I switched the UNAS Pro 8 to RAID 10 with six drives, meaning the same setup as the UNAS Pro, it was better across the board. The takeaway is that you can run RAID 5 or 6 with cache and get pretty close to RAID 10 performance while actually storing more data. With multiple RAID groups and hot spares supported, eight bays give you room for both.
 UniFi’s spec sheet lists two 550W power modules, which is the slot count, so you’d buy the second Hot-Swappable Power Module (550W) separately. For most home users, redundant power is something you don’t need. For a small business that wants SSD cache and redundant power in one box, it’s the right fit.
 I’ve compared every UniFi NAS model separately, including the seven-bay UNAS Pro.
 The 8-Bay Synology Pick: DS1825+ 
 Synology DS1825+: Best 8-Bay NAS for Synology DSM 
 AMD Ryzen V1500B · 8 GB DDR4 ECC (32 GB max) · 2x 2.5GbE · PCIe slot (up to 25GbE) · 8 bays + 2 M.2 (Synology SSDs) · expands to 18 bays
 The DS1825+ is the 8 bay Synology NAS to buy if you want DSM and its apps. It’s also the only one of my four picks that grows past eight bays, with up to two DX525 expansion units for 18 bays. The downside is the drive policy, which is better than it was but still limits M.2 SSDs.
 Check price at Amazon → 
 The PCIe slot takes a card up to 25GbE, and the two M.2 slots take Synology SSDs for cache or a storage pool. The Ryzen chip has no integrated graphics, so it isn’t the one to buy for Plex or Jellyfin transcoding.
 Synology’s drive policy has changed more than once, so this is where it stands as of September 2026. DSM 7.3 (released October 8, 2025) lets 2025 Plus models like the DS1825+, plus Value and J series, install non-validated third-party hard drives and create storage pools on them. M.2 storage pools and SSD cache still need drives from Synology’s compatibility list. DSM 7.4 (released June 16, 2026) then added Storage Efficiency, Synology’s post-process deduplication and compression, which requires Synology hard drives.
 Simply put, third-party hard drives work for storage pools, unlisted M.2 SSDs won’t work at all, and Storage Efficiency needs Synology drives . The product page still says Synology only guarantees full functionality with compatible drives. It runs the same DSM as the DS925+, which I still think is one of the best pre-built NAS devices you can buy, but the drive restrictions are the real issue on both.
 If you’re comparing the DS1825+ vs the DS1823xs+ , the xs+ model is still sold, with a faster Ryzen V1780B and 10GbE built in. It launched in 2023, so Synology’s 2025 drive policies don’t apply to it. If you’re set on Synology but not on eight bays, I’ve covered which Synology NAS you should buy across the lineup.
 QNAP and Asustor 8-Bay NAS Options 
 QNAP and Asustor both sell current 8-bay NAS devices, and they show up in almost every list. I haven’t tested either model, and they aren’t among my picks, but they cover two different tiers.
 QNAP TS-873A: 8 Bays With a ZFS Option 
 AMD Ryzen V1500B · 8 GB (64 GB max) · 2x 2.5GbE · 2x PCIe Gen3 slots for 10GbE · 8 bays + 2 M.2
 The TS-873A uses the same Ryzen V1500B as the DS1825+ and sits at about the same price tier. It takes up to 64 GB of memory, though, and can run QNAP’s ZFS-based QuTS hero instead of QTS. I’ve never been the biggest fan of QNAP’s operating system, since it isn’t as straightforward as Synology DSM, so I’d try QNAP’s online demo before buying.
 Check price at Amazon → 
 Asustor Lockerstor 8 Gen3 (AS6808T): 10GbE and Four M.2 Slots 
 AMD Ryzen Embedded V3C14 · 16 GB DDR5 ECC (64 GB max) · 2x 10GbE and 2x 5GbE · 2x USB4 · 8 bays + 4 M.2
 The AS6808T sits near the top of this list in cost. What the extra money buys over the QNAP and the Synology is DDR5 ECC memory, 10GbE built in, four PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots and two USB4 ports. It’s an AMD chip as well, so it isn’t the one for Plex or Jellyfin either.
 Check price at Amazon → 
 If you’re weighing QNAP against Synology more generally, I’ve compared the two platforms in Synology vs. QNAP .
 Do You Need 8 Bays, or Is a 6-Bay Enough? 
 If you think you’ll start with four drives, you probably don’t need an 8 bay NAS, and a six-bay like UGREEN’s DXP6800 Ultra is the better pick. The opposite mistake is buying a four-bay and filling it on day one. When it runs out, it’s not a simple upgrade. It is a full migration to a new device.
 An 8-bay makes sense when you already have a lot of data and know it’s growing. It also makes sense for two drives of parity (RAID 6 or RAID-Z2), which costs a quarter of your raw capacity on eight drives and a third on six. For a small business, the UNAS Pro 8 (with a second power module for redundancy) and the DXP8800 Ultra are the two I’d look at.
 Whichever one you buy, I’d budget for three things:
 Memory: almost all of these start with 8 GB of RAM (the AS6808T starts at 16 GB, and the UNAS Pro 8 runs no apps), so plan for more if you’ll run Docker or VMs.
 Networking: 10GbE does nothing for you unless your switch and the computer on the other end are 10GbE as well.
 Media: if you’re thinking Plex and Jellyfin, just buy an Intel device, meaning one of the UGREENs (see the best NAS for Plex ).
 If you’d rather build your own, an 8-bay NAS case is a different purchase. Otherwise, if you need a lot of data storage and you’re buying new, skip straight to the DXP8800 Ultra, because it’s the better overall device.

 What each column means
 Bays counts the 3.5-inch drive bays, which also take 2.5-inch drives. A model marked all-flash has no hard drive bays and holds only M.2 SSDs. M.2 is the number of M.2 NVMe slots free for your own SSDs. On most models these slots work as an SSD cache or as a separate storage pool. A slot that the maker fills with the system drive does not count.
 Max LAN is the fastest built-in Ethernet port. Some models add a second, slower port, and the chart lists only the faster one. Filter for 10GbE if you plan to move large files across a 10GbE network.
 ECC reads Yes only when the NAS supports ECC SO-DIMM memory modules. These modules carry extra check bits, so the processor can detect and correct memory errors, whether they happen inside a memory chip or on the way to the processor. DDR5 memory also has on-die ECC, which corrects errors only inside each memory chip, so the chart counts on-die ECC as No.
 Transcode reads Yes when the processor has a graphics engine that converts video in hardware. Media servers use it to stream to phones, TVs, and browsers that cannot play the original file. Jellyfin uses it on every model marked Yes; Plex support depends on the chip, as the transcoding section below explains. The Synology DS925+ reads No because its AMD Ryzen V1500B has no graphics engine.
 Idle is the power draw in watts with the NAS switched on and doing no work, as measured by the maker or a reviewer. The test conditions vary by source. Some figures have the hard drives spun down, some have no drives installed, and some have drives spinning. Synology measured the DS925+ at 12.33 W with four hard drives in hibernation, while the DXP6800 Pro figure of 22.4 W comes from a unit with no drives at all. Compare idle figures only when the conditions match, and check each product page for the conditions behind its number.

 Who needs a NAS
 A NAS (network-attached storage) is a small computer built to hold hard drives and share them over your home network. Every phone, laptop, TV, and streaming box on the network can reach the same files, and the NAS keeps running when your computers are off. The common jobs are phone photo backup, a backup target for Windows and Mac computers, a shared family drive, and a media library for Plex or Jellyfin. Newer models with faster chips also run Docker containers such as Home Assistant or Pi-hole, and a few virtual machines.
 You probably need one if your photos and documents live on a single laptop or a single USB drive, if two or more people need the same files, or if your media library has outgrown what a streaming box can hold. You probably do not need one if everything you care about already fits in a cloud plan you pay for and you have no media library. A NAS is also not the right tool for someone who wants no maintenance at all: every model in the chart needs updates, drive health checks, and a backup of its own.
 A NAS, a mini PC home server, or cloud storage
 Cloud storage is the simplest option. Google, Apple, and Microsoft keep the copies, handle the hardware, and give you access anywhere. The costs are a monthly fee that grows with your library, a copy of your files on someone else’s servers, and download speeds limited by your internet connection. Cloud storage also works as the off-site second copy for a NAS.
 A mini PC can do much of what a NAS does. It runs the same Linux, Docker, and Plex software, and it often has a faster processor for the money. It has little room for drives. A typical mini PC takes one or two M.2 SSDs and no 3.5-inch hard drives, so large libraries end up on USB enclosures. Our guides to using a mini PC as a NAS and building a mini PC home server cover that route.
 A NAS sits between the two. It holds two to eight hard drives, usually in hot-swap trays, protects them with RAID, and comes with software that handles sharing, backup, and photo sync without a Linux command line. Hard drives cost far less per terabyte than SSDs, so a NAS is the cheapest way to keep tens of terabytes at home. Several NAS models in the chart also have processors as fast as a mid-range mini PC, so one box can do both jobs.
 What a NAS operating system does
 The operating system decides more about daily life with a NAS than the hardware does. It sets which RAID types you can use, how backups work, which phone apps you get, and how long the box keeps receiving security fixes. Pick the software you want first, then find hardware that runs it.
 DSM, UGOS Pro, TOS, and MinisCloud OS
 Synology’s DSM runs only on Synology hardware and is the most complete NAS system in the chart. Its backup apps are the main reason to buy Synology: Hyper Backup makes versioned backups to another NAS, a USB drive, or cloud storage, and Active Backup for Business backs up Windows and Mac computers to the NAS. Synology Photos and Synology Drive cover phone photo backup and file sync. Our UGREEN vs Synology comparison goes through those apps in detail.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro runs on every NASync model. It is based on Debian and covers file sharing, a photo app with face and object recognition, file sync, Docker, and virtual machines. Its backup tools are thinner than Synology’s. TerraMaster’s TOS 7 includes TRAID (TerraMaster’s flexible RAID), Btrfs snapshots, a photo app, Docker with Portainer, and backup tools, but no built-in media center app. Minisforum’s MinisCloud OS is the newest of the four; ServeTheHome, Jim’s Garage, and Britec09 all called it unfinished in their N5 Pro reviews, and the first setup runs through a desktop or phone app rather than a web page.
 The DS925+ and the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus install their systems on the data drives. UGREEN puts UGOS Pro on its own eMMC chip or SSD (32GB of eMMC on the DXP2800, 64GB on the DXP4800 GT, and a 128GB SSD on the larger models), and the Minisforum units ship with a small system SSD in one of their M.2 slots. A separate system drive makes it easier to replace the operating system without touching your data.
 Synology’s drive rules
 Synology is the only maker in the chart with a drive compatibility list that decides what you can install. When the DS925+ launched in 2025, it would not install DSM on hard drives outside that list. Synology reversed course with DSM 7.3 on October 8, 2025 , and 2025 DiskStation Plus models now accept third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs for new storage pools.
 The M.2 slots are still restricted. Synology’s drive compatibility policy lists unlisted M.2 NVMe SSDs in DS Plus models as supported only when migrated from an older Synology system, not for new pools or caches. On a DS925+, that means Synology’s own NVMe SSDs if you want to use the M.2 slots at all. UGREEN, TerraMaster, Minisforum, and AOOSTAR have no drive list you have to follow.
 TrueNAS, Unraid, and Proxmox on NAS hardware
 Every model in the chart except the DS925+ is an x86 PC with drive bays that accepts a third-party system. TrueNAS Community Edition is free, runs on Debian, and is built on OpenZFS, with Docker apps and virtual machines. Unraid is a paid system that lets you mix drives of different sizes in one array and add drives one at a time. Proxmox is a virtual machine host, and some owners run TrueNAS inside a Proxmox virtual machine; Jim’s Garage set up the Minisforum N5 Pro that way.
 UGREEN allows third-party systems and keeps the hardware warranty, though it does not support the software, and on the DXP2800 and DXP8800 Plus you must disable a watchdog timer in the BIOS first. The 64GB eMMC system drive on the DXP4800 GT makes other installs less direct than on the UGREEN models with a system SSD. Minisforum supports Windows 11 and Linux on the N5 Air, and reviewers ran Windows 11, Proxmox, and TrueNAS on the N5 Pro. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U ships with no NAS system at all, so you bring your own from the start. The common snag across all of them is fan control: under TrueNAS or Unraid, the fans may run too fast or too slow until you set them up.
 A third-party system also protects you against the end of vendor updates. If the maker stops updating a model, TrueNAS or Unraid keeps running on standard x86 hardware. A Synology box runs DSM and nothing else in any supported way.
 Apps, Docker, and virtual machines
 Docker containers are small, self-contained apps: Home Assistant, Pi-hole, Immich for photos, a password manager, a download client. Every system in the chart runs them, and they need little processor power, but each one takes memory. A handful of containers fits comfortably in 8GB. The DS925+ ships with 4GB, which fills quickly once you add containers.
 Virtual machines are full operating systems running inside the NAS, such as a Windows desktop or a Linux test server. They need processor cores and several gigabytes of memory each. The DS925+, with four cores and 4GB installed, suits one small virtual machine at most. The Core i5 UGREEN models (10 cores), the AOOSTAR and the Minisforum N5 Air (6 or 8 cores), and the N5 Pro (12 cores) have room for several.
 NAS hardware
 Drive bays and capacity
 Bays set how much storage the NAS can hold and which RAID types it can use. Two bays give you a mirror: two drives with the same data, so one can fail. Four bays allow RAID 5, where one drive’s worth of space holds parity and the rest holds data, so four 12TB drives give about 36TB of usable space. RAID 6 survives two failed drives at the cost of two drives of space; it needs at least four drives but makes more sense with five or more, since four-drive RAID 6 leaves only half the raw space.
 For most homes, four bays are the practical minimum. A two-bay box such as the UGREEN DXP2800 costs less, but a mirror gives you only half the raw capacity, and to grow it you must replace both drives. Four bays let you start with three drives and add a fourth later. The chart has four-bay models from UGREEN, Synology, TerraMaster, and AOOSTAR, five-bay models from Minisforum, and six- and eight-bay models from UGREEN.
 Look at hot-swap trays too. Most models in the chart let you pull a failed drive while the NAS is running. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U does not, so you must shut it down to change a drive. The UGREEN DXP480T Plus has no drive bays at all: it holds four M.2 SSDs for up to 32TB of flash storage in a box about the size of a Mac mini.
 RAID, file systems, and why RAID is not a backup
 RAID keeps the NAS running when a drive fails. It does not protect you from deleting a file, from ransomware that encrypts your shares, from a power surge that kills every drive, or from a fire. Synology states it plainly in its knowledge base: “ RAID (classic and SHR) is not a backup solution .” The TrueNAS ZFS primer says the same: “RAID and disk redundancy are not substitutes for a reliable backup strategy.” The usual rule is 3-2-1 : three copies of your data, on two different media, with one copy off-site. For a NAS, that means a second copy on a USB drive or another NAS, and a third in cloud storage or at another house.
 Classic RAID 5 treats every drive as the size of the smallest one. Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR) combines drives of different sizes to use more of the space, and needs at least four drives for SHR-2, which survives two failures. TerraMaster’s TRAID works on the same idea. Unraid keeps a separate file system on each data drive and protects them with one or two parity drives, and Unraid’s documentation says the parity drive must be at least as large as the largest data drive. UGOS Pro offers standard RAID levels. MinisCloud OS builds only ZFS pools, so its choices are ZFS layouts: a stripe, a mirror, RAIDZ1 (similar to RAID 5), and RAIDZ2 (similar to RAID 6), which Minisforum lists as RAID 0, 1, 5, and 6.
 DSM, UGOS Pro, and TOS offer Btrfs, which supports snapshots: saved versions of a folder that you can roll back to after an accidental deletion or a ransomware attack, as long as the attack does not reach the snapshots themselves. They also offer ext4, which is simpler and has no snapshots. TrueNAS uses ZFS, which checksums every block it writes. When it finds a block that does not match its checksum on a mirrored or RAIDZ pool, it replaces the bad data with a good copy. DSM, UGOS Pro, and TOS do not use ZFS. MinisCloud OS on the Minisforum units uses ZFS only, with no Btrfs or ext4. On the other models you get ZFS by installing TrueNAS or a Linux distribution that supports it.
 CMR and SMR hard drives
 Buy NAS drives that use CMR (conventional magnetic recording). Some cheaper drives use SMR (shingled magnetic recording), which overlaps data tracks to fit more on a platter and slows down badly during long writes such as a RAID rebuild. Western Digital says on its blog that WD Red Plus is the name for its CMR NAS drives from 1TB to 14TB, while its 2TB to 6TB WD Red drives use device-managed SMR. TrueNAS found that one WD Red SMR model can enter a faulty state under heavy writes, including rebuilds, and recommends CMR drives.
 WD Red Plus, WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf, and Seagate IronWolf Pro are the common NAS lines, and each maker’s product page states the recording type. Check it before you buy, especially for drives of 6TB or less.
 M.2 slots for cache or a storage pool
 Most models in the chart have two or more M.2 NVMe slots. As a cache, the SSDs hold copies of files you open often so the NAS can serve them faster than the hard drives. As a separate storage pool, the SSDs become their own fast volume, which suits Docker apps and their databases. With apps on SSDs, the hard drives can spin down when nobody is using them, which saves power and noise.
 The lane count on each slot sets its top speed. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus gives each of its three M.2 slots one PCIe 3.0 lane, so one drive tops out just under 1,000 MB/s. The Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro run their free slots at x2 and x1, and the UGREEN DXP4800 GT at PCIe 3.0 x2. The DXP480T Plus runs two of its four slots at PCIe 4.0 x4. On most models the network is the slower link anyway, since a 2.5GbE port moves about 300 MB/s and a 10GbE port about 1,100 MB/s.
 Check what the M.2 slots accept before you count on them. On the DS925+, they take only Synology’s SSDs. On the AOOSTAR, which ships barebone, one of the two slots usually holds the operating system drive, which leaves one for data. The DXP480T Plus and DXP4800 Plus have no room for SSDs with their own full-height heatsinks.
 U.2 bays
 U.2 is a connector for data-center NVMe SSDs, which come in a 2.5-inch drive shape and reach larger capacities than M.2 drives. Two models in the chart accept them. On the UGREEN DXP4800 GT , bays 1 and 2 take a U.2 drive in place of a SATA drive, on a PCIe 3.0 x4 link. The Minisforum N5 Pro takes two U.2 drives through an included adapter in its data M.2 slots, limited to 7mm drives of up to 15TB, and the adapter replaces an internal fan. U.2 drives are enterprise SSDs, so this feature suits homelab owners who already have them.
